title: Beyond Abiotic Decay: Fiddler Crabs Accelerate Plastic Fragmentation in Pollution Hotspots
content:
Fiddler crabs are thriving in mangrove areas that are global hotspots of plastic pollution. Field experiments show that the amount of plastic they ingest is among the highest ever recorded in nature. About 15% of the ingested material is broken down into smaller pieces during digestion and released at detectable levels within just two weeks. This demonstrates that biological processes can drive plastic decay far more rapidly than environmental aging caused by sunlight, high temperatures, or friction, which occurs over decades. Such fragmentation produces microplastics that can interact with other contaminants, disperse more widely, enter food webs, and alter the fate of pollution in coastal ecosystems.


ABSTRACT

Mangrove forests are recognized as plastic sequestration hotspots, particularly in urbanized areas, which may contain up to two orders of magnitude more plastic litter. Fiddler crab populations, known as ecosystem engineers, are thriving precisely in these expanding plastic-pollution hotspots, prompting inquiry into how these creatures navigate the substantial plastic loads within sediments they have evolved to inhabit and feed upon. To investigate this, we released two types of unaged, fluorescently labeled polyethylene microspheres (hereafter, “microspheres”)—green (20–27 μm diameter) and red (75–90 μm diameter)—into polluted urban mangroves inhabited by the fiddler crab Minuca vocator. The microsphere sizes were chosen to mimic the natural range of food particle sizes encountered by these crabs. This field experiment tracked the uptake and fate of microspheres in the crabs' hepatopancreas, gills, hindgut, and the sediments over 66 days. Microspheres were incorporated by most crabs (91 out of 95), with uptake markedly higher in the hindgut (26.04 ± 1.19 SE microspheres g−1) and hepatopancreas (10.07 ± 1.19) than in the gills (0.86 ± 0.20). The average uptake of microplastics, 48.67 (±7.24 SE) per crab was more than 16 times higher than the density in the sediment (2.92 microspheres g−1), and represents one of the highest uptakes ever recorded in nature. Approximately 15% of this load, primarily located in the hepatopancreas, was found in a fragmented state, suggesting degradation through digestive processes. Microspheres fragmented by digestive processes were detectable in mangrove sediments within just 14 days, challenging the notion that plastic degradation is a long-term process driven mainly by abiotic aging over decades. Combined with the widespread presence of fiddler crabs along coastlines acting as plastic sinks, these findings suggest that biotic fragmentation is an important pathway for the degradation of plastics entering the ocean.

RESUMEN

Los bosques de manglar son reconocidos como puntos críticos en la acumulación de plástico, particularmente en áreas urbanizadas, donde se puede observar hasta dos órdenes de magnitud más residuos plásticos. Las poblaciones de cangrejos violinistas, que funcionan como ingenieros ecosistémicos, prosperan precisamente en estos sitios de alta concentración de plástico. Esto plantea interrogantes sobre cómo estos organismos, especializados evolutivamente para habitar y usar la matriz de sedimentos como sitio de alimentación interactúan con crecientes cantidades de materiales plásticos acumulados por décadas. Para investigarlo, liberamos microesferas de polietileno fluorescentes y no envejecidas, de tamaño similar al de las partículas alimenticias, en manglares urbanizados habitados por el cangrejo violinista Minuca vocator. Este experimento de campo permitió rastrear la incorporación y la transformación de los microplásticos en el hepatopáncreas, las branquias, el intestino posterior y los sedimentos durante 66 días. La incorporación promedio de microplásticos, 48.7 (±7.24 EE) por cangrejo, es una de las más altas registradas en condiciones naturales. Aproximadamente el 15% de esta carga, detectada principalmente en el hepatopáncreas, fue continuamente fragmentada. Las microesferas fragmentadas digestivamente fueron detectables en los sedimentos del bosque de manglar en tan solo 14 días, desafiando la noción de que la degradación del plástico es un proceso de largo plazo que opera mediante procesos de envejecimiento abiótico en escalas decadales. Junto con la amplia distribución de los cangrejos violinistas a lo largo de costas que actúan como sumideros de plástico, estos hallazgos sugieren que la fragmentación biótica es una vía importante para la degradación de los plásticos que ingresan al océano.
